title: Simulation Foundations: Systems, States, and Terminology
description: Canonical foundations from curriculum: system concepts, state variables, events/activities, and simulation methodology phases.

keyDetails.title: Curriculum anchor
keyDetails.content: Curriclum.docx syllabus and introduction define system/state terminology and the four problem-solving phases used through the semester.

keyDetails.title: Week 01 section support
keyDetails.content: Week 01 section slides reinforce foundational definitions before probability and queueing applications begin.

solvedProblems.title: Classify a system by behavior
solvedProblems.statement: Classify an ATM service desk as natural/man-made, deterministic/stochastic, and discrete/continuous.
steps: Identify origin: ATM is engineered by humans => man-made.
Check uncertainty: arrivals/service durations vary => stochastic.
Check state changes: queue length changes at events => discrete.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: ATM desk is man-made, stochastic, and discrete.

solvedProblems.title: State vector definition for single server
solvedProblems.statement: Define the minimal state for a one-server queue with FCFS service.
steps: Track server status (idle/busy).
Track number of customers waiting in queue.
Use arrivals/departures as event triggers updating these states.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Minimal state is (server status, queue length).

solvedProblems.title: Activity versus event distinction
solvedProblems.statement: In a machine-shop model, classify service time and machine breakdown as activity or event.
steps: Activity has duration; event is instantaneous.
Service process lasts over time => activity.
Breakdown occurrence changes state at an instant => event.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Service time is an activity; breakdown occurrence is an event.

title: Random Number Mapping for Discrete Outcomes
description: Build cumulative-probability intervals and map random numbers (00-99) to outcomes for manual simulation traces.

keyDetails.title: Mapping rule
keyDetails.content: Use cumulative intervals so each RN falls in exactly one outcome range (e.g., 00-09, 10-59, 60-99).

keyDetails.title: Course progression
keyDetails.content: This week operationalizes the Week 01 definitions into executable Monte Carlo traces.

solvedProblems.title: Discrete demand mapping from cumulative probability
solvedProblems.statement: Demand probabilities: D0=0.1, D1=0.5, D2=0.4. Determine demand for RN=42.
steps: Locate RN=42 in the table.
Read mapped outcome from interval 10-59.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Demand outcome is D1.

solvedProblems.title: Coin toss simulation mapping
solvedProblems.statement: For fair-coin simulation with RN in [0,1), map RN=0.73 and RN=0.18 to outcomes.
steps: Use rule: RN < 0.5 => Head, else Tail.
RN=0.73 is in [0.5,1) => Tail.
RN=0.18 is in [0,0.5) => Head.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Outcomes are Tail for 0.73 and Head for 0.18.

solvedProblems.title: Range-table construction check
solvedProblems.statement: Given probabilities [0.2, 0.3, 0.5], build 00-99 mapping intervals.
steps: Compute cumulative probabilities: 0.2, 0.5, 1.0.
Allocate first 20 numbers to outcome 1: 00-19.
Allocate next 30 numbers to outcome 2: 20-49, remaining 50 to outcome 3: 50-99.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Intervals are 00-19, 20-49, and 50-99.

title: Monte Carlo Trial Execution and Frequency Stability
description: Run repeated trials and compute empirical frequencies, then compare to expected theoretical probabilities.

keyDetails.title: Section 3 evidence
keyDetails.content: Simulation-Section_3 focuses on two-digit random numbers and mapped outcome frequencies.

keyDetails.title: Evaluation focus
keyDetails.content: Students verify that simulation frequencies approach expected probabilities as trials increase.

solvedProblems.title: 100-trial fair coin estimate
solvedProblems.statement: Estimate P(Head) using 100 Monte Carlo draws.
steps: Generate 100 independent RN values.
Count heads where RN<0.5.
Divide head count by 100.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Empirical estimate approaches 0.5 with enough trials.

solvedProblems.title: Convergence comparison across sample sizes
solvedProblems.statement: Compare error from 20 trials versus 200 trials for same Bernoulli process.
steps: Compute p-hat at n=20 and n=200.
Measure absolute error against theoretical probability.
Observe lower variability for n=200.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Larger sample size gives a more stable, lower-error estimate.

solvedProblems.title: Empirical demand distribution from traces
solvedProblems.statement: From simulated demands [0,1,2,1,1,2,0,1,2,1], estimate probabilities.
steps: Count each demand value occurrences.
Convert counts to proportions by dividing by 10.
Report empirical distribution and compare to input distribution.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Estimated probabilities are P(0)=0.2, P(1)=0.5, P(2)=0.3.

title: Case Simulation I: Accident and Football Risk Problems
description: Apply Monte Carlo logic to contextual case studies with loss/injury outcome distributions.

keyDetails.title: Accident case
keyDetails.content: Accident Problem.pdf models stochastic accident penalties using discrete probability levels.

keyDetails.title: Football case
keyDetails.content: Football problem.pdf applies simulation to player-injury impact over games and roster availability.

solvedProblems.title: Accident frequency simulation (12 days)
solvedProblems.statement: Use Week 4 accident table (2-6 accidents/day with given probabilities) to simulate 12 days.
steps: Convert accident probabilities into cumulative RN intervals.
Map 12 random numbers to daily accident counts.
Sum and average daily accidents from the simulated horizon.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: A complete 12-day trace yields estimated mean accidents/day from mapped outcomes.

solvedProblems.title: Football running-backs choice problem
solvedProblems.statement: From the Week 4 football problem, select running back outcomes according to probability ranges.
steps: Build RN intervals for the six running backs.
Map each generated RN to one running back outcome.
Summarize frequencies to support decision comparison.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Mapped frequencies approximate the original running-back probabilities.

solvedProblems.title: Reorder-point trigger with random lead time
solvedProblems.statement: Stock starts at 12, reorder point=5, daily demand [2,3,4,1,2], lead-time drawn from distribution.
steps: Update end-of-day stock after each demand.
Place order when stock <= reorder point and no outstanding order.
Schedule order arrival using sampled lead-time and continue trace.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Order is triggered once stock crosses the threshold and arrives after sampled lead time.

title: Distributions and Multi-Stage Decision Simulation
description: Connect distribution basics (mean/variance) with branch-dependent simulation logic such as insurance decision trees.

keyDetails.title: Section 5 scope
keyDetails.content: Week 05 materials include distribution formulas and staged simulation logic in one progression.

keyDetails.title: Decision-tree modeling
keyDetails.content: Insurance-style branch simulation demonstrates conditional probability handling in manual traces.

solvedProblems.title: Insurance call two-stage simulation
solvedProblems.statement: Using section-5 rules: RN1=30 (interest), RN2=85 (policy type), determine sale outcome.
solvedProblems.method: Conditional branching with two RN streams
steps: Map RN1 against interest range (00-49 => interested).
Since interested, map RN2 against policy-type intervals.
Read final branch outcome from second-stage range.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Outcome is a large policy sale.

solvedProblems.title: Expected policy value over 20 calls
solvedProblems.statement: Simulate 20 house calls and estimate expected policy value per call.
solvedProblems.method: Repeated branch simulation with payoff averaging
steps: For each call, execute interest branch then sale-type branch.
Assign payoff (no sale, small policy, large policy) by outcome.
Average total payoff over 20 calls.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Expected value is total simulated revenue divided by 20 calls.

solvedProblems.title: Discrete vs continuous distribution moments
solvedProblems.statement: From Section 5 Problem 1, compute mean and variance for one discrete and one continuous example.
steps: For discrete X: compute E[X]=Σxp(x) and Var[X]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2.
For continuous X: compute E[X]=∫xf(x)dx and Var[X]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2.
Evaluate numerically for provided parameters in the sheet.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Mean and variance follow standard discrete/continuous moment definitions.

title: Time-Advance Methods: Periodic Scan vs Event Scan
description: Introduce simulation clock management and compare fixed-increment scanning with next-event advancement.

keyDetails.title: Section 6 objective
keyDetails.content: Session3_Performance identifies Section 6 as the transition to time-advance mechanisms for discrete-event systems.

keyDetails.title: Method trade-off
keyDetails.content: Event scan improves efficiency by jumping to real event times instead of checking empty ticks.

solvedProblems.title: Periodic versus event-scan timeline
solvedProblems.statement: Events occur at t=3 (arrival) and t=8 (departure). Compare checks for Δt=1 periodic scan vs event scan.
steps: Periodic scan evaluates times 0 through 8 each tick.
Event scan jumps directly to t=3 then t=8.
Count checks/events processed by each method.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Event scan processes only real event times and needs fewer checks.

solvedProblems.title: Future Event List ordering
solvedProblems.statement: Given FEL entries D@12, A@7, A@10, process next two events.
steps: Sort FEL by smallest event time.
Execute A@7 then update state and schedule any follow-up event.
Execute next earliest event from updated FEL.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Events are handled in chronological order: A@7 then A@10 (before D@12).

solvedProblems.title: Single-server state update on arrival/departure
solvedProblems.statement: Server idle at t=0, arrivals at t=1 and t=2, service time=3 each. Trace queue length and server status.
steps: At t=1 first arrival starts service immediately.
At t=2 second arrival joins queue since server is busy.
At t=4 first departure occurs, queued job starts service.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Queue builds to length 1 at t=2 and drains when first service completes at t=4.

title: Queue Inputs and Random Variate Preparation
description: Prepare queue simulations using CDF-based random observation generation for core distributions.

keyDetails.title: Week 07 file evidence
keyDetails.content: Simulation-Section_7 extraction references deriving CDF and random-observation equations for U(a,b) and Exp.

keyDetails.title: Midterm boundary
keyDetails.content: The 7th-week exam materials indicate this week closes the first half of the course sequence.

solvedProblems.title: Two-customer waiting-time trace
solvedProblems.statement: C1 arrives at 1, service 3; C2 arrives at 2, service 2. Compute waits and average wait.
steps: C1 starts at 1 and departs at 4 (wait=0).
C2 starts at 4 and departs at 6 (wait=2).
Average wait=(0+2)/2.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Average waiting time is 1 time unit.

solvedProblems.title: Queue length profile from event list
solvedProblems.statement: Arrivals at [0,1,3], departures at [2,5,7]. Determine queue length just after each event.
steps: Start from empty system.
Increment system count at arrival and decrement at departure.
Record queue length considering one active server.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Queue length evolves by cumulative arrivals minus departures minus in-service customer.

solvedProblems.title: Average waiting time from full trace
solvedProblems.statement: Waiting times are [0,1,4,2,3] minutes. Compute average and identify worst case.
steps: Divide by customer count 5 to get average.
Find max wait by scanning list.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Average wait is 2 minutes; worst-case wait is 4 minutes.

title: Revision and Validation Tables (Chi-Square/KS Support)
description: Consolidate first-half topics and practice statistical validation support using proof sheets and standard tables.

keyDetails.title: Revision evidence
keyDetails.content: Week 08 directory is explicitly labeled Revision and contains simulation proof sheets plus Z-table reference.

keyDetails.title: Validation continuity
keyDetails.content: Curriculum syllabus names Chi-square and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests; this week supports those computations.

solvedProblems.title: Chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic
solvedProblems.statement: Observed [12,18,20,10], expected [15,15,15,15]. Compute χ².
steps: Compute each contribution (Oi-Ei)^2/Ei.
Add all four contributions.
Use DOF and alpha table for accept/reject decision.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: χ² = 5.6 before comparing to critical value.

solvedProblems.title: Kolmogorov-Smirnov maximum gap
solvedProblems.statement: For empirical CDF [0.2,0.55,0.8,1.0] and theoretical [0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0], compute D.
steps: Compute |F_emp-F_theory| at each point.
Select maximum as KS statistic D.

solvedProblems.title: Z-table lookup for standardized value
solvedProblems.statement: Find P(Z<1.25) and right-tail probability using Z-table.
steps: Read cumulative value at z=1.25 from table (≈0.8944).
Compute right tail as 1-0.8944.
Interpret as exceedance probability.

title: 7th Exam Debrief and Integrated Trace Review
description: Work through 7th exam answer sets to consolidate random mapping, queue traces, and interpretation quality.

keyDetails.title: Folder evidence
keyDetails.content: Week 09 is organized as 7th Exam Answer, indicating a dedicated debrief/review week.

keyDetails.title: Learning purpose
keyDetails.content: Students compare method steps against answer keys to remove procedural mistakes before advanced cases.

solvedProblems.title: Policy comparison under same demand stream
solvedProblems.statement: Compare inventory policies RP=5 and RP=8 under identical daily demands.
steps: Run both policies with same random demand sequence.
Track stockouts and average inventory for each policy.
Compare service level versus holding burden.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Higher reorder point usually lowers stockouts and raises average stock.

solvedProblems.title: Stockout-day counting
solvedProblems.statement: Given ending stocks [3,1,0,-1,4,0], count stockout days and stockout ratio.
steps: Mark day as stockout when ending stock <= 0.
Count marked days in horizon.
Divide by total days to obtain ratio.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Stockout occurred on 3 of 6 days (50%).

solvedProblems.title: Average inventory level from trace
solvedProblems.statement: Daily ending stocks are [10,8,7,5,9]. Compute average inventory.
steps: Divide by 5 days.
Interpret result as average carrying level.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Average inventory is 7.8 units.

title: Machine Maintenance and Replacement Simulation
description: Model equipment failure/repair and evaluate maintenance and replacement timing through simulated traces.

keyDetails.title: Section text signal
keyDetails.content: Week 10 full solution describes a maintenance problem for complex equipment with component failures.

keyDetails.title: Decision objective
keyDetails.content: Simulation outputs are used to compare maintenance policy performance before implementation.

solvedProblems.title: Server utilization from busy time
solvedProblems.statement: Busy time is 45 minutes over a 60-minute run. Compute utilization.
steps: Use rho = busy time / total time.
Substitute 45/60.
Convert to percentage.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Utilization is 0.75 (75%).

solvedProblems.title: Idle time and percentage
solvedProblems.statement: If total run is 8 hours and busy time is 5.5 hours, compute idle time and idle percent.
steps: Idle time = total - busy = 2.5 hours.
Idle fraction = 2.5/8.
Convert to percentage.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Idle time is 2.5 hours, i.e., 31.25%.

solvedProblems.title: Failure-repair queue interpretation
solvedProblems.statement: In the week-10 full-solution context (frequent tube failures), explain effect of higher failure rate on queue metrics.
steps: More failures increase arrival rate to repair queue.
If service capacity unchanged, waiting and queue length rise.
Higher waiting raises downtime and may lower effective throughput.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Higher failure intensity worsens waiting, queue length, and downtime unless repair capacity is improved.

title: Two-Stage Assembly Line (Bob and Ray)
description: Simulate tandem service stations, identify waiting buildup, and quantify bottleneck effects.

keyDetails.title: Primary case
keyDetails.content: Week 11 files explicitly focus on the two-stage Bob-and-Ray assembly line simulation.

keyDetails.title: Performance interpretation
keyDetails.content: Service-rate mismatch is analyzed through trace tables to explain queue buildup and lost throughput.

solvedProblems.title: Bob-Ray bottleneck identification
solvedProblems.statement: In two-stage line, Bob=3 min/item and Ray=5 min/item. Identify bottleneck.
steps: Convert times to rates: Bob 20 items/hr, Ray 12 items/hr.
Lower processing rate determines bottleneck.
Infer queue buildup before slower stage.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Ray (stage 2) is bottleneck.

solvedProblems.title: Line utilization by stage
solvedProblems.statement: Total run is 120 min. Bob busy 90 min, Ray busy 110 min. Compute stage utilizations.
steps: Bob utilization = 90/120.
Ray utilization = 110/120.
Compare values to explain where congestion forms.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Bob utilization is 75%; Ray utilization is about 91.7%, confirming Ray as tighter stage.

solvedProblems.title: Throughput estimate for serial stations
solvedProblems.statement: Given deterministic stage times 4 min then 6 min/item, estimate long-run throughput.
steps: Compute capacities: stage1=15/hr, stage2=10/hr.
Serial line throughput limited by minimum capacity.
Use slower stage as long-run output rate.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Throughput is limited to about 10 items/hour.

title: Repairman Capacity Models (One vs Two Repairmen)
description: Compare maintenance queues under different repair capacity levels and interpret downtime-cost tradeoffs.

keyDetails.title: Week 12 package
keyDetails.content: Week 12 includes dedicated One Repairman and Two Repairman solution files for direct comparison.

keyDetails.title: Operational insight
keyDetails.content: Capacity expansion is evaluated via simulated waiting, repair completion, and downtime costs.

solvedProblems.title: One-repairman Tucson Mills interpretation
solvedProblems.statement: For One Repairman sheet, discuss expected queue and downtime behavior under random breakdowns.
steps: Model breakdowns as arrivals and repairs as service times.
With one repairman, jobs can queue during clustered failures.
Queued repairs increase machine downtime cost.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: One repairman creates higher waiting and downtime risk when failures cluster.

solvedProblems.title: Two-repairman capacity effect
solvedProblems.statement: Compare one versus two repairmen when downtime cost is $40/hour per failed machine.
steps: Estimate waiting reduction from adding second repair server.
Translate reduced waiting to lower downtime hours.
Compute cost impact via $40 per machine-hour down.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Two repairmen usually reduce queueing delay and downtime cost substantially.

solvedProblems.title: Repair queue KPI extraction
solvedProblems.statement: From a repair trace, breakdown arrivals=15, completed repairs=14 in horizon with average wait 1.8h. State interpretation.
steps: Unfinished jobs imply residual backlog at horizon end.
Average wait indicates repair responsiveness level.
Use both to decide if extra capacity is justified.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: System is near capacity: one unresolved job and 1.8h average wait suggest pressure on maintenance resources.

title: Queueing Performance Integration: Time-Driven vs Event-Driven
description: Finalize by computing M/M/1 performance measures and comparing time-driven and event-driven implementations on the same queue.
concepts: M/M/1 metrics (P0, L, Lq, W, Wq)

keyDetails.title: Week 13 evidence
keyDetails.content: Event Driven.pdf and Time Driven.pdf share the same M/M/1 prompt, requiring side-by-side simulation approaches.

keyDetails.title: Course closure
keyDetails.content: week 13 simulation.pdf integrates queue equations, trace execution, and performance interpretation in one capstone week.

solvedProblems.title: M/M/1 performance measures derivation
solvedProblems.statement: Derive P0, Pn, L, Lq, W, Wq for M/M/1 and evaluate at rho=0.8.
steps: Use P0=1-rho and Pn=(1-rho)rho^n.
Compute L=rho/(1-rho), Lq=rho^2/(1-rho).
Using Little's law, compute W=L/lambda and Wq=Lq/lambda.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: At rho=0.8: P0=0.2, L=4, Lq=3.2, with W and Wq from lambda scaling.

solvedProblems.title: Time-driven versus event-driven selection
solvedProblems.statement: For irregular queue arrivals, choose simulation clock strategy and justify.
steps: Time-driven scans many empty ticks when events are sparse.
Event-driven jumps directly between actual event times.
Prefer method minimizing unnecessary state checks.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: Event-driven simulation is preferred for irregular sparse arrivals.

solvedProblems.title: Integrated simulation pipeline design
solvedProblems.statement: Outline full workflow combining RN generation, mapping, event logic, and metric reporting for final assignment.
steps: Generate random variates and map to interarrival/service outcomes.
Run event calendar (arrivals/departures) while updating state variables.
Collect KPIs (L, W, utilization), then validate against theory/tests.
solvedProblems.finalAnswer: A complete solution links random inputs, event processing, KPIs, and validation in one reproducible simulation run.
